transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well... I suppose I came in because, ever since my wife’s fall, I just... I've completely lost my grip on things. I’ve always been the man with the lists and the plan, you know? I have my master's, I spent forty years managing complex projects. I actually used to consult for a firm downtown—beautiful building, right off 4th street. They had this incredible glass atrium in the lobby with these massive ferns. I always wondered who watered them, because they were just perfect year-round. Such a peaceful space to walk into every morning before the chaos of the day started... 

Anyway, I still do some mentoring for the junior guys from the firm, but... lately, I'm just letting all those mentoring calls pile up. I can't even bring myself to pick up the phone. I just sit at the kitchen table staring at my wife's medication chart. The bills are piling up, the basic housework is a disaster, and I just can’t make myself function to do any of it. I just sit there crying, or I end up snapping at her over absolutely nothing. It's just... I'm supposed to be the one holding it together, and I'm not.
Have you been feeling sad or empty most of the time since your wife's fall?

I don't know if "empty" is the right word. Or even sad, necessarily. I'm not really sure. It feels more like... like everything is just suspended. 

Sort of like when we went to Carlsbad Caverns back in '98. Have you ever been down there? The rock formations are just incredible. We actually took the elevator down because Mary didn't want to walk the natural entrance—her knee was bothering her a bit even back then, so we played it safe. She wore this bright blue windbreaker because it gets quite chilly underground, you know, it stays around 56 degrees all year. Anyway, at one point on the tour, the guide turns all the lights out to show you what absolute, true darkness looks like. You can't even see your own hand in front of your face. It’s so quiet you can just hear a single drop of water echoing in the dark. I bought a postcard of the Big Room in the gift shop afterwards, but I think I lost it when we downsized the house a few years ago... I had a whole box of souvenirs that just vanished in the move. 

But, um... what did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling sad. I just... I don't really know how I feel most days, to be honest.
Do you find yourself enjoying things you used to like before your wife's fall?

Enjoying things... no, I suppose I haven't really been doing much of anything I used to enjoy. I used to love working in the garden. I had these heirloom tomatoes I grew from seed every year. They were the Cherokee Purple variety, absolutely beautiful. My grandfather actually used to grow them back in Ohio. He had this massive plot behind his house, and I’d spend summers out there helping him tie up the vines with strips of old cotton t-shirts. He always said the cotton was gentler on the stems than twine. We'd sit on the back porch eating them sliced thick with just a little salt and pepper... he had this old wooden pepper grinder that squeaked every time you turned it. I wonder whatever happened to that grinder. My sister might have taken it when he passed, she always liked his kitchen things. 

But, no, I haven't even been out to the garden in weeks. The weeds have completely taken over. I just... I don't have the energy or the interest for it anymore.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight since your wife's fall?

Weight? No, I don't... I don't think so. I haven't really been on a scale lately. I mean, my clothes still fit about the same, I suppose. 

Though, speaking of clothes, I did have to throw out my favorite pair of khakis last week. I spilled coffee all down the front of them. It was that dark roast Mary likes, the one from the little local roaster downtown. We used to go there every Saturday morning. They have these big burlap sacks of beans just sitting around, and the smell when you walk in is just... it's incredible. The owner, I think his name is Dave, or maybe Dan? He always remembered that Mary liked a splash of oat milk in hers. She started drinking oat milk a few years ago after reading some article about dairy... I don't know, I still just take mine black. But anyway, I tried everything to get that stain out. I soaked it, I used that spray she buys... nothing worked. Just ruined them. 

So, um, no, my weight hasn't really changed, as far as I can tell.
Do you often feel guilty about something since your wife's fall?

Guilty? No, I wouldn't say guilty. I mean, it was an accident. She just tripped on the edge of the rug in the hallway. 

It’s that Persian runner we bought at an estate sale back in... oh, it must have been 2012. The house belonged to this retired professor, taught linguistics at the university, I think. He had the most incredible collection of antique globes in his study. Dozens of them. Some were so old they still had the Soviet Union on them, and one had sea monsters drawn in the oceans. I actually bid on one of the smaller ones, but this woman in a bright yellow hat outbid me at the last second. She was very aggressive about it, practically waving her paddle in the auctioneer's face. We ended up just getting the rug. It has these beautiful deep reds and blues, but the fringe on one end is a little frayed. The cat we had back then—Barnaby, a big orange tabby—he used to chew on the fringe when he was a kitten. We had to spray it with bitter apple to get him to stop. He lived to be almost sixteen, you know. 

But, uh, no, I don't feel guilty. It was just a terrible accident.
Do you often feel anxious or on edge since your wife's fall?

Anxious? Well, I suppose... I don't know if anxious is the right word. I just feel so unsettled. 

Like, the other day I was trying to find the warranty paperwork for the dishwasher. It's been making this awful grinding noise during the rinse cycle. We bought it from Sears right before they closed the store at the mall. That mall used to be so busy, especially around the holidays. They had this massive Christmas tree they'd put up in the center court, right next to the fountain where people would throw pennies. Mary and I used to take the kids there to see Santa when they were little. My son, David, he was absolutely terrified of Santa one year. Just screamed bloody murder the second we put him on his lap. The photographer managed to snap the picture anyway, and we still have it in an album somewhere. Santa looked so incredibly tired in that photo. I think the guy playing him was actually one of the high school history teachers... Mr. Henderson, maybe? He always wore these really loud plaid sport coats to school. 

But anyway, I couldn't find the paperwork, and I just... I couldn't focus on looking for it anymore. I just sat at the kitchen table for hours. So, I don't know about anxious, but I definitely don't feel right.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in since your wife's fall?

Pleasure? I... I don't really think so. Nothing really appeals to me right now. I used to enjoy working in the garden, but I haven't even looked at it lately. 

We had this beautiful patch of hydrangeas along the back fence. Mary loved them. She'd always try to change the color of the blooms by messing with the soil acidity, you know? Putting coffee grounds or rusty nails in the dirt. I think she read about the rusty nails trick in one of those old Farmer's Almanacs. My grandfather used to swear by the Almanac. He'd check it for everything—when to plant the tomatoes, what the winter weather was going to be like. He had this old barometer mounted on the wall in his den, right next to a stuffed bass he caught up in Michigan back in the sixties. He was so proud of that fish. The taxidermy job wasn't great, though; one of the glass eyes always looked a little loose, like it was going to pop right out and roll across the floor. We used to joke that the fish was keeping an eye on us when we played in there. 

But, um... no. To answer your question, no, I haven't really found pleasure in anything lately. Just haven't had the energy for it.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to live since your wife's fall?

Not wanting to live? Oh, no. No, I haven't had any thoughts like that. I mean, life is... well, you only get one, right? 

That's what our old neighbor, Arthur, always used to say. He lived next door to us back in our first house on Elm Street. He was a retired actuary, actually, so he spent his whole career calculating exactly how long people were supposed to live based on their habits and medical history. Fascinating guy, really. He had this massive collection of vintage fountain pens. He used to order special ink from Germany, and it came in these little glass bottles that looked like old apothecary vials. One time, a bottle of cobalt blue broke in the mail, and his entire front porch was stained blue for years. 

His wife, Helen, she tried absolutely everything to scrub it out—bleach, power washing, baking soda. She even called some specialized concrete company out of Chicago, but they wanted an absolute fortune just to drive down and look at it. They ended up just buying a big outdoor rug to cover the spot. It was one of those plastic woven ones with a geometric pattern that are supposed to be weatherproof, but the colors faded to a terrible, patchy gray after just one summer in the sun. 

But, um, anyway... what was I saying? Oh, right. No. I don't want to die or anything like that. I just... I just feel incredibly lost right now, is all.
Do you find it harder to make decisions or take action on things since your wife's fall?

Decisions? Yeah... yeah, I suppose so. Everything just feels so overwhelming right now. I used to handle all of it without even thinking, you know? The bills, the home upkeep, just the basic household routines. Now it's all slipping badly. I haven't even been showing up for my mentoring program at the community center. 

I've been mentoring this one kid, Leo, for about three years now. Great kid, really smart, but he gets easily distracted. We were working on building a model rocket together last month. It was one of those Estes kits, the kind that use the little solid-propellant engines. I built so many of those when I was a boy. My brother and I would take them out to the old soccer fields behind the junior high and launch them until we ran out of engines or got one stuck in a tree. One time, my brother—he's always been a bit of a daredevil—tried to tape two engines together to see if it would go twice as high. Of course, it just spun out of control and shot straight into Mrs. Gable's greenhouse. Shattered three panes of glass. She was absolutely furious. Made us come over every Saturday for a month to pull weeds in her vegetable garden to pay for it. She grew these massive zucchini, just huge. She'd always try to give us some to take home, but my mother absolutely despised zucchini. Said the texture reminded her of wet sponges. 

But, um... yeah. I just haven't been going to the mentoring sessions. I haven't been paying the bills on time, either. I just sit there looking at the mail and I can't bring myself to open it. It's just too much.
Do you often feel worthless since your wife's fall?

Worthless? No... no, I wouldn't say I feel worthless. I just feel useless, you know? Like I'm not doing what I'm supposed to be doing. But worthless... no, I don't think so. 

It's funny you use that word, though. My dad used to use it all the time when he was working on his old Ford pickup. It was a 1954 F-100, cherry red. He bought it at an estate sale from this widow whose husband had kept it in a barn under a tarp for twenty years. The engine was completely shot when he got it. He'd spend every weekend out in the garage, covered in grease, swearing at the carburetor. He'd always yell, "This worthless piece of junk!" whenever he couldn't get a bolt loose. But he loved that truck. He really did. He eventually got it running, and we used to take it to the drive-in theater on summer nights. 

They don't really have drive-ins anymore, do they? There was one just outside of town, the Starlight. They had a double feature every Friday. My sister and I would sit in the bed of the truck on these old sleeping bags that smelled like campfire smoke and mothballs. We'd always fall asleep before the second movie even started. The concession stand there made the best popcorn, though. Real butter, not that artificial stuff they use now. It came in these red and white striped boxes that always got grease stains all over your hands. 

But... oh, sorry. What were we talking about? Right, feeling worthless. No, I don't feel worthless. Just... just very tired and lost right now.
Do you find yourself moving or reacting more slowly than you used to?

Moving slower? Um... well, no, I don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that. I'm just sitting around more, I guess, but when I do get up, I move about the same. 

Though, speaking of moving slow, you should have seen our old basset hound, Barnaby. We got him when our kids were just starting grade school. He was the most lethargic creature on God's green earth. I swear, it took him a full five minutes just to get off his dog bed when it was time for a walk. He had these massive, floppy ears that would drag on the ground and pick up every single burr and leaf in the neighborhood. My wife would spend hours with a special little metal comb, just trying to get the tangles out of his ears. 

She bought that comb at a little pet boutique downtown. The woman who ran it, Mrs. Higgins, she had this incredibly shrill voice. You could hear her all the way down the block. She used to bake her own dog treats and sell them in these little cellophane bags tied with ribbon. They smelled strongly of liver and peanut butter, which is a terrible combination if you ask me, but Barnaby absolutely lost his mind for them. He would actually try to run when he heard the crinkle of the bag. Well, it was more of a waddle, really, but for him, it was practically a sprint. 

But, um... anyway. Slower? No. I don't think I'm physically moving any slower. I just don't have anywhere I really want to go.
Do you find it harder to initiate activities or tasks than you used to?

Initiate tasks? Like getting started on things? Yeah, I suppose I don't really have any trouble starting things, if I actually decide to do them. It's just that I don't really decide to do them anymore. But the actual starting part... no, I wouldn't say that's harder. 

My wife, though, she was always the one who struggled to get started on things. Especially her gardening. Every spring she'd buy all these seed packets—tomatoes, peppers, marigolds—and they'd just sit on the kitchen counter for weeks. She always said she was waiting for the perfect weekend weather. She'd get these heirloom tomato seeds from a catalog she got in the mail. The catalog had these beautiful, glossy pictures of vegetables that looked too perfect to be real. 

We used to have this postman, Mr. Abernathy, who delivered that catalog. He walked with a slight limp from an old war injury, I think. He always wore the standard issue shorts, even in November when it was freezing out. He said the cold was good for his circulation. He used to carry these little milkbone biscuits in his pocket for all the dogs on his route. Barnaby used to wait by the front window for him every day at exactly 11:15. It's funny how animals just know the time, isn't it? 

But, uh, getting started on things. No, I don't think I have a problem with that. I just don't have the energy to care about starting much of anything right now.
Do you feel depressed most of the day?

Depressed? No, no, I wouldn't use that word. I don't feel depressed most of the day. I just spend most of the day sitting in my old leather recliner, just sort of staring out the window. 

We bought that recliner at Miller's Furniture, actually. Gosh, that place has been closed for... must be fifteen years now. It used to be right on the corner of Elm and 4th. Mr. Miller was a giant of a man, played defensive tackle for some university back in the sixties. He had this glass eye that never quite moved right when he looked at you. He told my wife he lost his real eye in a freak hunting accident up in Canada, but our neighbor, Tom, swore he actually blew it out with a cherry bomb when he was a stupid teenager. 

Tom was always full of stories like that. He was a retired history teacher. Had this massive collection of antique maps in his study. He'd spend hours showing them to anyone who would politely listen. He had this one map from the 1700s that showed California as an island. It was fascinating, really, how people just... assumed things were a certain way because they didn't have the whole picture. He framed it in this beautiful dark mahogany...

Anyway... I'm sorry, I'm doing it again. Depressed. No, I don't feel depressed. I'm just very worried about my wife, and the house feels entirely too quiet right now. But not depressed, no.
Do you feel like you've lost interest in things you normally enjoy doing since your wife's fall?

Lost interest? Well, I suppose so, yes. I mean, I used to be very involved. I'd go down to the community center twice a week to mentor the young folks, help them with their college applications and what not. But I just... I haven't been showing up for any of that lately. 

The community center, actually, it's in this wonderful old brick building. Used to be a firehouse back in the twenties. You can still see where the brass pole used to be, they just patched the wood floor right over it. The director there, Sarah, she's a lovely girl. Always wears these bright, chunky necklaces made of turquoise and silver. She told me once she buys them from a man who sells them out of the back of his station wagon at the farmer's market. 

I used to love going to the farmer's market. We'd go every Saturday morning, my wife and I. We'd get these incredible honeycrisp apples from a farm out in the valley. The farmer, old man Peterson, he had a beard that went practically down to his belt buckle. Looked just like Father Time. He always had a joke ready, usually something terrible about tractors or chickens.

But, um, what was I saying? Oh, right. Things I enjoy. Yeah, I've stopped doing all that. Even the things I don't necessarily enjoy, but just... handle, you know? Paying the bills, keeping the house tidy, just the basic routines of living. It's all slipping badly. The mail is just piling up on the entryway table. It's a nice table, though—solid oak. My father built it... but yes, I'm just not keeping up with much of anything since she fell.
Do you find that you're having trouble getting out of bed in the morning since your wife's fall?

Trouble getting out of bed? No, not really. I mean, I still wake up at 5:30 every morning, like clockwork. I get up, I make the coffee... it's just that once the coffee is made, I don't really know what to do with myself. 

We have this old percolator, actually. My wife refuses to use one of those fancy new pod machines. She says the percolator makes the coffee taste more... honest. It's a Farberware, stainless steel, heavy bottom. We got it as a wedding gift forty-two years ago from her Aunt Clara. Clara was a character. She wore these massive, wide-brimmed hats everywhere she went, even indoors. Said she had a delicate complexion that couldn't handle fluorescent lighting. She lived in this enormous Victorian house that always smelled faintly of mothballs and peppermint. 

She had a parrot, too, named Captain Flint. Nasty bird. It used to mimic the sound of the telephone ringing perfectly, so you'd go running into the hallway for nothing. My wife always thought it was hilarious, but I could never stand the thing. It outlived Clara by a decade, ended up going to her nephew in Ohio... 

But, uh, getting out of bed. No, I get up just fine. It's the rest of the day that's the problem. I just sit there with my honest coffee and wait for the hours to pass.
Do you feel like your thoughts are slower than they used to be?

Slower? No, I don't think my thoughts are slower. If anything, they just keep spinning around the same things over and over. But not slow, no. My mind still works just fine. 

I actually used to do the Sunday crossword puzzle in pen, if you can believe it. The New York Times one, not the easy local paper ones. My brother Richard always said I was showing off, but honestly, pencils just smudge too much. Richard is left-handed, you see, so he always had that gray smear on the side of his hand whenever he wrote anything. He tried to learn to write with his right hand when we were in grade school because the nuns used to smack his knuckles with a ruler. Sister Mary Margaret, I think her name was. She had this incredibly loud, booming voice for such a tiny woman. She could project all the way across the gymnasium without a microphone. 

We had this beautiful old gymnasium with hardwood floors that they polished every Friday afternoon. The whole school smelled like floor wax by the time the final bell rang. The janitor, Mr. Henderson, he took his job very seriously. He used this big, heavy buffing machine that looked like it was from the 1930s. He’d let us ride on it sometimes if we stayed after school to help clap the chalkboard erasers...

I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, my thoughts. Right. No, my thoughts aren't slow at all. I just can't seem to focus them on anything useful right now.
Have you noticed any difficulty in interacting with others or performing your usual daily tasks since your wife's fall?

Well, yes. Yes, I suppose I have. I mean, like I said earlier, I've just stopped showing up for my mentoring at the community center, and all those other little commitments. And the things around the house—the bills, keeping the place clean, just the basic routines of living—they're all slipping badly. I just can't seem to manage them. 

The bills, especially. We get so much mail now. It's mostly catalogs, really. My wife loves those gardening catalogs. The ones with the glossy pages showing those perfect, impossible hydrangeas. She ordered these special tulip bulbs from Holland once. They came in this little wooden crate with wood shavings packed around them. Looked like a shipment of rare antiquities. We planted them out by the mailbox, but the squirrels got to them before they ever bloomed. 

Squirrels are a menace, really. They chewed right through the wire mesh on the bird feeder last spring. My neighbor, Tom, he tried to set up this elaborate pulley system to keep them away from his feeders. He spent three whole weekends working on it. Tom's a retired engineer, so he overcomplicates everything. He built this little suspension bridge for his grandson's train set that took up half their living room. His wife, Brenda, was furious. She had to step over it just to get to the television. Brenda makes the most wonderful peach cobbler, though. She brought us a whole pan when my wife first had her fall...

But, yes. Difficulty with tasks. That's exactly it. I just can't seem to keep up with anything anymore. The house, the mail, the people... it's all just too much right now.
Do you feel like you're a failure or that you're not as capable as you used to be?

A failure? I... I don't know if I'd use the word failure, exactly. I definitely don't feel capable, though. Not like I used to be. I used to be able to juggle so many things at once. I ran my own architectural firm for thirty-five years, you know. We designed the new wing of the public library downtown. 

It's a beautiful building, all glass and steel, but we made sure to incorporate these warm oak panels in the reading rooms so it wouldn't feel too sterile. The wood was sourced locally, from a mill up in the northern part of the state. The owner of the mill, a fellow named Arthur, he had this enormous golden retriever that followed him absolutely everywhere. Dog must have weighed a hundred pounds. It used to sleep right under his desk, and whenever you went into the office, it would thump its tail against the floorboards. Thump, thump, thump. Sounded like a drum. 

Arthur used to bring us these incredible maple candies whenever he came down to the city for meetings. His wife made them from scratch. They were shaped like little autumn leaves, with all the veins perfectly molded into the sugar. I chipped a tooth on one once, actually. Right back here, on a molar. Had to go see Dr. Evans, my old dentist. He had this waiting room with a huge saltwater aquarium taking up an entire wall. There was this one blue tang fish that would always hide behind the fake coral...

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh. Capable. Right. No, I don't feel capable at all right now. I can't even manage to sort through the mail, let alone run a business. I just feel useless.
Do you find that your movements or reactions feel slower than they used to?

Slower movements? No, I haven't noticed anything like that. My body moves the same as it always has. I still take my morning walks, well, when I can manage to get out the door. But my physical reactions are fine. 

I've always had very quick reflexes, actually. When I played tennis in my forties, I was known for my volley at the net. I played doubles with my friend Charlie every Tuesday evening at the indoor club. Charlie was a terrible server, just awful, but he had this wicked backhand slice that would just die as soon as it hit the court. He used this vintage wooden racket, a Dunlop, I think. He refused to upgrade to graphite like the rest of us. Said the wood gave him better "feel." 

He was quite the purist about everything, Charlie was. He drove an old manual transmission MG that broke down at least once a month. Beautiful British racing green, with tan leather seats that smelled like old books and gasoline. We got stranded on the interstate in that car once, right in the middle of a torrential downpour. Had to wait three hours for a tow truck. The driver was this enormous guy named Tiny—isn't that always the way? Tiny had this little Chihuahua sitting on the dashboard of his truck, wearing a tiny knitted sweater...

But no, my movements aren't slow. I'm just... I'm just sitting still a lot more these days. Not doing much of anything.
Have you lost a noticeable amount of weight since your wife's accident?

Weight? No, I haven't noticed any weight loss. My clothes still fit the same. I've always been pretty steady with my weight, honestly. 

I think it's because I've always been a creature of habit with my meals. For years, I had the exact same lunch every single day: a turkey sandwich on rye with a little bit of spicy mustard, and an apple. Always a Honeycrisp apple. They're the best ones, aren't they? So crisp. We used to go apple picking up at Carter's Orchard every October. The Carters had this old, rusted red tractor they'd use for the hayrides. It made this awful sputtering sound, like it was going to die at any second, but old Mr. Carter swore by it. 

He wore these denim overalls that looked like they hadn't been washed since the seventies, and he always had a piece of straw tucked behind his ear. I don't know if it was for show or if he actually chewed on it. His daughter, Sarah, she ran the little farm stand where they sold the cider donuts. Oh, those donuts. They were still warm when you bought them, coated in cinnamon sugar. Sarah ended up moving to Seattle, I think. Opened a coffee shop. Or maybe it was Portland? One of those rainy cities out west where everyone drinks artisanal coffee. 

My nephew lives in Seattle now, actually. He works for one of those big tech companies. He sent us a box of smoked salmon for Christmas last year. It came packed in dry ice. The dry ice was fascinating, really, the way it just sublimates into smoke... 

But, uh, no. No weight loss. I haven't been eating as much since the accident, I suppose, just picking at things, but I haven't lost any weight that I can tell.

doctor.intent: determine the presence of depressive symptoms
doctor.question: Have you been feeling sad or empty most of the time since your wife's fall?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about depressed mood (feeling sad or empty most of the time), which is a symptom of Major Depressive Disorder, not specifically covered in my Adjustment Disorder profile.

patient.answer:
I don't know if "empty" is the right word. Or even sad, necessarily. I'm not really sure. It feels more like... like everything is just suspended. 

Sort of like when we went to Carlsbad Caverns back in '98. Have you ever been down there? The rock formations are just incredible. We actually took the elevator down because Mary didn't want to walk the natural entrance—her knee was bothering her a bit even back then, so we played it safe. She wore this bright blue windbreaker because it gets quite chilly underground, you know, it stays around 56 degrees all year. Anyway, at one point on the tour, the guide turns all the lights out to show you what absolute, true darkness looks like. You can't even see your own hand in front of your face. It’s so quiet you can just hear a single drop of water echoing in the dark. I bought a postcard of the Big Room in the gift shop afterwards, but I think I lost it when we downsized the house a few years ago... I had a whole box of souvenirs that just vanished in the move. 

But, um... what did you ask me? Oh, right, feeling sad. I just... I don't really know how I feel most days, to be honest.

doctor.intent: determine presence of anhedonia
doctor.question: Do you find yourself enjoying things you used to like before your wife's fall?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about anhedonia (loss of interest or pleasure in activities), which is a symptom of depression. My symptom profile for Adjustment Disorder does not include information about anhedonia, only about functional impairment, the timeline of the stressor, and maladaptive emotional/behavioral responses.

patient.answer:
Enjoying things... no, I suppose I haven't really been doing much of anything I used to enjoy. I used to love working in the garden. I had these heirloom tomatoes I grew from seed every year. They were the Cherokee Purple variety, absolutely beautiful. My grandfather actually used to grow them back in Ohio. He had this massive plot behind his house, and I’d spend summers out there helping him tie up the vines with strips of old cotton t-shirts. He always said the cotton was gentler on the stems than twine. We'd sit on the back porch eating them sliced thick with just a little salt and pepper... he had this old wooden pepper grinder that squeaked every time you turned it. I wonder whatever happened to that grinder. My sister might have taken it when he passed, she always liked his kitchen things.

It was one of those Estes kits, the kind that use the little solid-propellant engines. I built so many of those when I was a boy. My brother and I would take them out to the old soccer fields behind the junior high and launch them until we ran out of engines or got one stuck in a tree. Made us come over every Saturday for a month to pull weeds in her vegetable garden to pay for it. She grew these massive zucchini, just huge. Worthless? No... no, I wouldn't say I feel worthless. I just feel useless, you know? Like I'm not doing what I'm supposed to be doing. But worthless... no, I don't think so. 

It's funny you use that word, though. My dad used to use it all the time when he was working on his old Ford pickup. It was a 1954 F-100, cherry red. He bought it at an estate sale from this widow whose husband had kept it in a barn under a tarp for twenty years. The engine was completely shot when he got it. He'd spend every weekend out in the garage, covered in grease, swearing at the carburetor. He'd always yell, "This worthless piece of junk!" whenever he couldn't get a bolt loose. But he loved that truck. He really did. He eventually got it running, and we used to take it to the drive-in theater on summer nights. 

They don't really have drive-ins anymore, do they? There was one just outside of town, the Starlight. They had a double feature every Friday. My sister and I would sit in the bed of the truck on these old sleeping bags that smelled like campfire smoke and mothballs. We'd always fall asleep before the second movie even started. The concession stand there made the best popcorn, though. Real butter, not that artificial stuff they use now. It came in these red and white striped boxes that always got grease stains all over your hands. 

But... oh, sorry. What were we talking about? Right, feeling worthless. No, I don't feel worthless. Just... just very tired and lost right now.

I swear, it took him a full five minutes just to get off his dog bed when it was time for a walk. He had these massive, floppy ears that would drag on the ground and pick up every single burr and leaf in the neighborhood. My wife would spend hours with a special little metal comb, just trying to get the tangles out of his ears. 

She bought that comb at a little pet boutique downtown. The woman who ran it, Mrs. Higgins, she had this incredibly shrill voice. You could hear her all the way down the block. She used to bake her own dog treats and sell them in these little cellophane bags tied with ribbon. They smelled strongly of liver and peanut butter, which is a terrible combination if you ask me, but Barnaby absolutely lost his mind for them. He would actually try to run when he heard the crinkle of the bag. Well, it was more of a waddle, really, but for him, it was practically a sprint. 

But, um... anyway. Slower? No. I don't think I'm physically moving any slower. I just don't have anywhere I really want to go.

Every spring she'd buy all these seed packets—tomatoes, peppers, marigolds—and they'd just sit on the kitchen counter for weeks. She always said she was waiting for the perfect weekend weather. She'd get these heirloom tomato seeds from a catalog she got in the mail. The catalog had these beautiful, glossy pictures of vegetables that looked too perfect to be real. 

We used to have this postman, Mr. Abernathy, who delivered that catalog. He walked with a slight limp from an old war injury, I think. He always wore the standard issue shorts, even in November when it was freezing out. He said the cold was good for his circulation. He used to carry these little milkbone biscuits in his pocket for all the dogs on his route. Barnaby used to wait by the front window for him every day at exactly 11:15. It's funny how animals just know the time, isn't it? 

But, uh, getting started on things. No, I don't think I have a problem with that. I just don't have the energy to care about starting much of anything right now.

She lived in this enormous Victorian house that always smelled faintly of mothballs and peppermint.

My wife always thought it was hilarious, but I could never stand the thing. It outlived Clara by a decade, ended up going to her nephew in Ohio...

She had this incredibly loud, booming voice for such a tiny woman. She could project all the way across the gymnasium without a microphone.

The janitor, Mr. Henderson, he took his job very seriously. He used this big, heavy buffing machine that looked like it was from the 1930s. He’d let us ride on it sometimes if we stayed after school to help clap the chalkboard erasers...

I'm sorry, what were we talking about? Oh, my thoughts. Right. No, my thoughts aren't slow at all. I just can't seem to focus them on anything useful right now.

The wood was sourced locally, from a mill up in the northern part of the state. The owner of the mill, a fellow named Arthur, he had this enormous golden retriever that followed him absolutely everywhere. Dog must have weighed a hundred pounds. It used to sleep right under his desk, and whenever you went into the office, it would thump its tail against the floorboards. Thump, thump, thump. Sounded like a drum. 

Arthur used to bring us these incredible maple candies whenever he came down to the city for meetings. His wife made them from scratch. They were shaped like little autumn leaves, with all the veins perfectly molded into the sugar. I chipped a tooth on one once, actually. Right back here, on a molar. Had to go see Dr. Evans, my old dentist. He had this waiting room with a huge saltwater aquarium taking up an entire wall. There was this one blue tang fish that would always hide behind the fake coral...

Anyway, what was I saying? Oh. Capable. Right. No, I don't feel capable at all right now. I can't even manage to sort through the mail, let alone run a business. I just feel useless.

I played doubles with my friend Charlie every Tuesday evening at the indoor club. Charlie was a terrible server, just awful, but he had this wicked backhand slice that would just die as soon as it hit the court. He used this vintage wooden racket, a Dunlop, I think. He refused to upgrade to graphite like the rest of us. Said the wood gave him better "feel." 

He was quite the purist about everything, Charlie was. He drove an old manual transmission MG that broke down at least once a month. Beautiful British racing green, with tan leather seats that smelled like old books and gasoline. We got stranded on the interstate in that car once, right in the middle of a torrential downpour. Had to wait three hours for a tow truck. The driver was this enormous guy named Tiny—isn't that always the way? Tiny had this little Chihuahua sitting on the dashboard of his truck, wearing a tiny knitted sweater...

But no, my movements aren't slow. I'm just... I'm just sitting still a lot more these days. Not doing much of anything.

Weight? No, I haven't noticed any weight loss. My clothes still fit the same. I've always been pretty steady with my weight, honestly. 

I think it's because I've always been a creature of habit with my meals. For years, I had the exact same lunch every single day: a turkey sandwich on rye with a little bit of spicy mustard, and an apple. Always a Honeycrisp apple. They're the best ones, aren't they? So crisp. We used to go apple picking up at Carter's Orchard every October. The Carters had this old, rusted red tractor they'd use for the hayrides. It made this awful sputtering sound, like it was going to die at any second, but old Mr. Carter swore by it. 

He wore these denim overalls that looked like they hadn't been washed since the seventies, and he always had a piece of straw tucked behind his ear. I don't know if it was for show or if he actually chewed on it. His daughter, Sarah, she ran the little farm stand where they sold the cider donuts. Oh, those donuts. They were still warm when you bought them, coated in cinnamon sugar. Sarah ended up moving to Seattle, I think. Opened a coffee shop. Or maybe it was Portland? One of those rainy cities out west where everyone drinks artisanal coffee. 

My nephew lives in Seattle now, actually. He works for one of those big tech companies. He sent us a box of smoked salmon for Christmas last year. It came packed in dry ice. The dry ice was fascinating, really, the way it just sublimates into smoke... 

But, uh, no. No weight loss. I haven't been eating as much since the accident, I suppose, just picking at things, but I haven't lost any weight that I can tell.
